morph.note: With roots of motion and a few others (√स्था among them) the past participle can be active and take an object: माहिषं वपुः आस्थितः ‘having assumed the buffalo body’, not ‘placed’.
Taddhita noun from त्रिलोक (‘the three worlds’) with vṛddhi of the first syllable (त्रि → त्रै): the three worlds taken as one whole.
Periphrastic perfect of the causative of √क्षुभ् (guṇa u → o): ‘caused to tremble’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः महासुरः भूयः माहिषं वपुः आस्थितः (सन्) तथा एव सचराचरं त्रैलोक्यं क्षोभयामास।
mantras.lit: Then the great asura, having again taken on (his) buffalo body, in just the same way shook the three worlds with (all) that moves and does not move.
mantras.tr: Then the great demon took on his buffalo body once more and, as before, threw the three worlds into turmoil, all that moves and all that stands still.

comm.t: After lion, man and elephant the asura returns to the buffalo, and the cosmic disorder of 3.25–27 begins again (तथैव ‘just as before’). The circle of transformations is closed; the next move is the Goddess’s.

mantras.anvaya: ततः क्रुद्धा अरुणलोचना जगन्माता चण्डिका उत्तमं पानं पुनः पुनः पपौ, जहास च एव।
mantras.lit: Then the enraged Mother of the world, Caṇḍikā, drank the supreme drink again and again, and indeed laughed, red-eyed.
mantras.tr: Then Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the world, in her fury drank the supreme drink again and again, and laughed, her eyes red.

comm.t: The Goddess drinks and laughs in the face of the asura’s renewed onslaught. The drink is called only ‘the supreme drink’ here; she herself calls it मधु in 3.38. The drinking-vessel is one of her gifts in chapter 2: Kubera gave her a cup never empty of wine (ददावशून्यं सुरया पानपात्रं धनाधिपः, 2.30).
The Goddess’s drinking and laughter before the kill are read in the Śākta tradition as signs of her fierce form and of her ease: the battle is play to her (cf. लीलयैव, 3.4).

The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also pictures the Goddess with eyes reddened by intoxication: name 432, मदघूर्णितरक्ताक्षी, ‘whose red eyes roll with intoxication’. The image is shared; the context there is not a battle.

samasa.vigraha: बलं च वीर्यं च बलवीर्ये; तयोः मदः बलवीर्यमदः; तेन उद्धतः
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (outer), containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (बलवीर्यमद) and an itaretara dvandva (बलवीर्य)
samasa.literal: puffed up by the intoxication of strength and valour
samasa.sense: arrogant, drunk on his own strength

morph.note: Perfect of √नर्द्: reduplication न-; the root has no guṇa or vṛddhi to take (a heavy syllable).
As a karmapravacanīya प्रति follows its accusative and gives direction: चण्डिकां प्रति ‘at Caṇḍikā’.

mantras.anvaya: बलवीर्यमदोद्धतः सः असुरः अपि ननर्द च, विषाणाभ्यां चण्डिकां प्रति भूधरान् चिक्षेप च।
mantras.lit: And that asura too, swollen with the pride of strength and valour, bellowed, and with (his) two horns hurled mountains at Caṇḍikā.
mantras.tr: The demon, drunk with pride in his strength and valour, roared back and with his horns flung mountains at Caṇḍikā.

comm.t: Laughter and roar answer each other: she laughs (जहास, 3.34), he bellows (ननर्द). Two kinds of intoxication stand face to face — her drink and his मद, the pride of strength.
A modern reading: the text puts the same word, मद, on the asura’s pride. The intoxication that matters in the story is his: he cannot see what he is fighting.

words.g: n. acc. sg. used adverbially (kriyāviśeṣaṇa); compound (see Samāsa); qualifies उवाच

sandhi.note: Final n before t becomes ṃs: प्रहितांस्तेन.

samasa.members: मद + उद्धूत + मुख + राग + आकुल + अक्षर
samasa.vigraha: मदेन उद्धूतः मदोद्धूतः; मुखस्य रागः मुखरागः; मदोद्धूतः मुखरागः मदोद्धूतमुखरागः; तेन आकुलानि अक्षराणि यस्मिन् (कर्मणि) तत् यथा तथा
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi used as an adverb (outer); inside it a karmadhāraya (मदोद्धूतमुखराग) of a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (मदोद्धूत) and a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (मुखराग), and a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (…रागाकुल)
samasa.literal: in a manner in which the syllables were confused by the facial flush stirred up by intoxication
samasa.sense: her words thick with the drink, her face flushed
samasa.alt: It can also be read as a masculine accusative agreeing with तम्: Mahiṣa, ‘whose speech was confused by the flush of his face stirred up by pride (मद)’. The adverbial reading is preferred: it is the Goddess who has just drunk (3.34) and who speaks; the asura has only bellowed.

morph.note: Present participle of a curādi root (stem चूर्णय-) with the feminine suffix -ई: चूर्णयत् → चूर्णयन्ती. Her action runs while she speaks: ‘pulverising … she said’.
Past participle of प्र + √हि: the i of the root is kept (हित), not the participle of √धा.
A neuter accusative singular can describe the manner of an action (kriyāviśeṣaṇa): ‘she spoke in such a way that …’. उद्धूत is the past participle of उद् + √धू ‘to shake up, stir’.

mantras.anvaya: सा च तेन प्रहितान् तान् शरोत्करैः चूर्णयन्ती मदोद्धूतमुखरागाकुलाक्षरं तम् उवाच।
mantras.anvaya_en: A present participle of accompanying action (चूर्णयन्ती) with its own object, then the main verb उवाच with its person addressed (तम्) and an adverbial compound of manner.
mantras.lit: And she, pulverising with volleys of arrows those (mountains) hurled by him, spoke to him in a manner in which (her) syllables were confused by the flush of (her) face stirred up by intoxication.
mantras.tr: Grinding to dust with volleys of arrows the mountains he hurled, she spoke to him, her face flushed with the drink and her words slurred:
mantras.tr_note: The long compound is taken as an adverb describing her speech; the alternative (describing the asura) is given in Samāsa.

comm.t: The verse introduces the Goddess’s only direct speech in the chapter (3.38). She speaks while still destroying his missiles: the words and the arrows come together.
Translators differ over whose face is flushed. Most take the compound with the Goddess, who has just drunk; it can grammatically describe the asura instead (see Samāsa).

flags.uncertain: The reference of मदोद्धूतमुखरागाकुलाक्षरम् (the Goddess’s speech, adverbial; or the asura, agreeing with तम्) is an interpretive choice; the adverbial reading is preferred.
